payload.claim: For a ±10% Bitcoin grid bot with 20 levels (W≈0.20, δ≈1%, fee=0.1%) at 36% annualized volatility, the expected net monthly return on a random walk is approximately -0.5% of capital, equal to the fee cost.
payload.quote: Take a ±10% Bitcoin grid with 20 levels: W ≈ 0.20, δ ≈ 1%, f = 0.1%. At 36% annual volatility, daily σ is about 1.9%, so 30 days of squared moves add up to about 0.0107. The harvest is 0.0107 × C/2W (= 2.5) × 0.8 ≈ 2.1% of capital. On a random walk the expected cost is 0.0107 × 2.5 ≈ 2.7%. Net: about −0.5% a month, which is exactly the fees.

payload.text:
gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-intraday-daily-marks: intraday strategies are simulated per bar and measured on daily marks.

Rule. An intraday strategy (timeframe below 1d, session 24x7 only) is simulated bar by bar: vol-target sizing annualises with bars per year (365 x bars per day), short financing accrues per bar, the volatility-percentile regime window is 365 days of bars. Every statistic the gauntlet records or gates on is computed on the equity curve marked once per UTC day (the last bar of each date): the Sharpe floor's train Sharpe, the asset volatility that normalises edge per trade, the effective-trials clustering series, the deflated Sharpe and haircut inputs, the walk-forward folds and the regime labels, and the screen's recorded max drawdown. Trade-based gates (edge per trade, edge decay, Monte Carlo p05, ruin, cost stress) are unchanged. A daily strategy's bars are its daily marks, so every daily verdict before and after this note is computed identically.

Quarantine and the live gate. An intraday strategy's forward record is one quarantine_decision per cell per UTC day, written at the day's last bar: the cell is named ASSET@TF (for example BTCUSDT@1h) in the row's asset field and in that day's data snapshot; price, position and equity are the book at the day's last bar; the row adds entries and exits, the trades the strategy opened and closed that day. A UTC day with at least one bar is complete when the cell's last bar of the day is on disk, or when any later bar is; a UTC day with no bars at all is never recorded (a hole in the file). The live gate counts closed forward trades as the sum of exits over these rows, and a trading day for a 24x7 strategy is a UTC calendar day. Daily strategies' rows are unchanged.

crypto-grid-phase2-v1: Phase 2 of the chained crypto-grid-record-v1 grid is active from this entry: timeframes 1h, 4h and 12h on the same 76 assets, 228 cells. It adds no cell outside that grid, changes no existing verdict and re-judges nothing on the chain. Intraday statistics follow gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-intraday-daily-marks, chained just before this note.

THE CELLS. Phase 1's 76 cells (1d) were active from the grid record. With the 228 cells of this entry, 304 of the grid's 456 cells are active. The cells are the same 76 assets in the grid record's manifest order, each at 1h, 4h and 12h, and nothing else. Phase 3 (15m and 30m) stays inactive until its own Coen-gated commit.

THE EXCLUSION RULE. The grid record excludes a phase 2 cell whose own first bar falls after 2022-12-31. That rule was applied to every one of the 228 cells and excludes none, because every phase 2 cell's own first bar falls on or before 2022-12-31. The latest first bar of any phase 2 cell is APTUSDT, 2022-10-19. Every intraday price file starts no earlier than its asset's 1d file, so no cell's history reaches back past the history its asset was admitted on.

WHAT COUNTS. Each phase 2 cell is its own counted trial. Activating this phase adds its cells to what is searched. More registrations at a fixed bar is arithmetic about the denominator, never evidence of edge.

payload.claim: In China, the staggered introduction of ambient air quality monitoring in a city causes financial analysts based in that city to become substantially more likely to discuss air pollution in their coverage.
payload.quote: Exploiting the staggered rollout of China's ambient air quality monitoring program, we show that when monitoring is introduced in a city, analysts based there become substantially more likely to discuss air pollution.

source.title: Pollution Monitoring and the Pricing of Environmental Risk in Firms -- by Namrata Kala, Jalal Sani, Nemit Shroff, Pengdong Zhang

data_required: dates of city-level rollout of China's ambient air quality monitoring program
analyst report text/coverage data by analyst location and firm
classification of analyst location by city
testability.notes: Requires textual analysis of analyst reports to measure pollution discussion frequency.

payload.claim: Stock market reactions to analyst reports issued by analysts treated by the introduction of ambient air quality monitoring are more negative for brown firms, more positive for green firms, and largely unchanged for environmentally neutral firms, relative to reactions to reports from untreated analysts.
payload.quote: These changes in attention are reflected in stock prices: reports issued by treated analysts generate more negative market reactions for brown firms and more positive reactions for green firms, with little change for environmentally neutral firms.

source.title: Pollution Monitoring and the Pricing of Environmental Risk in Firms -- by Namrata Kala, Jalal Sani, Nemit Shroff, Pengdong Zhang

data_required: analyst report issuance dates and analyst location
stock price/return data around report dates
firm classification into brown/green/neutral based on environmental exposure
testability.notes: Core asset-pricing event-study claim distinguishing by firm environmental type.

payload.claim: The stock price reactions to reports issued by treated analysts regarding brown and green firms' environmental risk do not reverse in subsequent periods.
payload.quote: These price responses do not subsequently reverse.

source.title: Pollution Monitoring and the Pricing of Environmental Risk in Firms -- by Namrata Kala, Jalal Sani, Nemit Shroff, Pengdong Zhang

data_required: stock returns for brown/green firms following treated analyst reports
testability.notes: Tests for absence of mean-reversion in the price impact identified in the prior claim.

payload.claim: Following the introduction of ambient air quality monitoring in their city, analysts increase corporate site visits and issue less favorable assessments of brown firms and more favorable assessments of green firms compared to untreated analysts.
payload.quote: Treated analysts increase their information acquisition through corporate site visits and issue less favorable assessments of brown firms and more favorable assessments of green firms.

source.title: Pollution Monitoring and the Pricing of Environmental Risk in Firms -- by Namrata Kala, Jalal Sani, Nemit Shroff, Pengdong Zhang

data_required: analyst report favorability/rating data by firm type (brown/green)
testability.notes: Covers both information acquisition (site visits) and output (report favorability) channels.

payload.claim: In a month-by-maturity panel of U.S. Treasuries from 1988 to 2024, expected excess bond returns (measured using market yields and professional forecasts) have a 67% correlation with bonds' betas with respect to the stock market.
payload.quote: We measure expected excess returns using market yields and professional forecasts of future yields, showing that they are tightly linked to a standard measure of risk: bonds’ betas with respect to the stock market. In a month-by-maturity panel of U. S. Treasuries from 1988 to 2024, the correlation between expected excess returns and bond–stock betas is 67%.

source.title: Risk and Return in Government Bonds -- by Matteo Leombroni, Carolin Pflueger, Adi Sunderam

data_required: U.S. Treasury market yields by maturity 1988-2024
testability.notes: Decomposition claim relying on the same panel described in the preceding sentence.

payload.text:
gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-2: Amends gauntlet-protocol-v6.1, chained at registry entry 68486, and gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-1, chained at registry entry 81246, in one thing the gauntlet_stats entries record: how the effective trials count is made. From this note onward it is counted per cell partition, by one average-linkage tree per partition cut at a fixed correlation of 0.9, and the partitions' counts are summed. Everything else in v6.1 and amendment-1 stands as written: the floor on trials_n, the floor on SR*, the series the deflated Sharpe is computed on, PBO, plateau_ok and the haircut formula. No gate is added, removed or re-tuned, no threshold moves, and no verdict or state change is touched. Pre-declared before the first per-cell gauntlet_stats entry exists: pipeline/gauntlet_stats.py refuses to chain any gauntlet_stats entry until this note is on the chain.

WHY. Until this note the statistics job clustered every registered strategy in one pass and picked k by the silhouette argmax. That pass holds one n x n float64 matrix over all n registered strategies, and the job starts it only when free physical memory covers it. n grows by hundreds of registrations a day, so the pass would stop fitting within weeks. A memory cut of the same method that gives bit-identical results is not possible: a row-blocked distance matrix differs in the last bit and changes the merge history (measured 2026-11-01). So the count itself changes. Per partition, the matrix held at any time is the largest partition's, not the whole registry's.

THE METHOD. Step 1: the aligned series are built exactly as before (intersection when asset classes are mixed or calendars are ragged, native otherwise): the same rows, the same days, the same length L. Step 2: the rows are split into partitions by cell key, the strategy's cells sorted and joined by "|". A multi-asset strategy (the legacy BTCUSD and ETHUSD pair) is its own partition, and an intraday strategy's key carries its timeframe (BTCUSDT@1h), so an intraday strategy and its daily original sit in different partitions. Step 3: in each partition, the rows that never trade in the aligned window (every value exactly 0.0) are taken out before the tree and form ONE cluster of their own, when the partition has any; its representative Sharpe is 0.0. A row that is constant but not zero makes the whole run refuse: exit 1, exit_reason cluster_refused, nothing chained. Step 4: the remaining rows of each partition get the merge history of the unchanged clustering code (pipeline/cluster.py: the same correlation distance, the same average linkage, the same deterministic tie-break), and each merge's height is read: the average-linkage distance between the two clusters at the moment they merge. Step 5: each partition's tree is cut at the distance t = sqrt(0.5 x (1 - 0.9)), the distance that corresponds to a correlation of 0.9. A merge counts when its height rounded to 12 decimals is at or under t rounded to 12 decimals. The counted merges are the merges in order up to the first one over t; a later merge at or under t (float noise) does not count, and the run reports how many there were as cut_late_merges, in its status file and run log only. A partition's k is its remaining rows minus its counted merges, plus 1 when it has never-traded rows; a partition of one strategy has k = 1. Step 6: trials_n_raw is the sum of the partitions' k. Step 7: the cluster labels are made global by taking the partitions in sorted key order and offsetting each partition's labels by the k of the partitions before it. Step 8: trials_sr_var is the sample variance of every cluster's representative Sharpe (the mean daily Sharpe of its members) pooled over all partitions in one sample; the never-traded cluster of a partition enters it once. Step 9: the floors, SR*, the deflated Sharpe and the haircut are computed by the unchanged code from steps 6 and 8: trials_n is the larger of trials_n_raw and the highest cluster count on the chain, and SR* is floored as amendment-1 says. The deflated Sharpe is still computed on the registry-wide aligned series. The silhouette search is no longer run by the statistics job. The correlation 0.9 is a named constant, CUT_RHO, recorded on every entry; CUT_RHO changes only by a new chained note, never as a tuning knob.

WHAT EACH ENTRY RECORDS. cluster_method is "effective_trials/v4 per-cell average-linkage cut rho>=0.9" (it was "effective_trials/v3 correlation-distance"). Three fields are added: trials_partitions (the number of partitions), trials_largest_partition_n (the strategy count of the largest one) and trials_cut_rho (0.9). Every other field is recorded as before. The full per-partition table goes to the job's report file, and the 20 largest partitions to its run log; neither goes onto an entry. The trials_n floor still reads trials_n_raw from earlier gauntlet_stats entries and the cluster counts of v3 to v6 verdicts; the list of protocols it reads is unchanged.

MEASURED. On a copy of the chain read on 2026-11-05, re-statting the 300 verdicts the 2026-11-05 01:00 run statted, on the same registry (30,140 registered strategies), the same data vintage (2026-11-01) and the same data, with nothing chained: 111 partitions, 36 of them intraday; the largest is IWM with 1,068 strategies; L is 1,003 days. The per-cell count gives trials_n_raw 6,183, trials_sr_var 0.001293 and SR* 0.13453. The registry-wide method on the same inputs that night recorded k 4,320, trials_sr_var 0.0011789 and SR* 0.12533; that k and that SR* are also the chain floors (trials_sr_var has no floor), so both floors sit below the per-cell figures and an entry would record the per-cell ones. There were 375 never-traded rows in 15 partitions, no constant nonzero row and no late merge. An independent average-linkage implementation (scipy) cut at the same distance gave the same k in all 111 partitions. Every one of the 300 recorded deflated Sharpe values falls: the median from 1.42e-5 to 3.83e-6. None is at or above 0.95, before or after. The clustering added 332 MB of memory; the per-cell gate's own estimate was 391 MB at the real L and 570 MB at the gate's bound on L, where the registry-wide pass needed 9,831 MB by the job's own estimate.

RATCHET POSITION. No gate reads trials_n, SR*, the deflated Sharpe, PBO, plateau_ok or the haircut, under v6.1, amendment-1 or here, so nothing a gate decides changes. A higher count and a higher SR* can only lower the recorded deflated Sharpe and raise the recorded haircut: stricter, never more lenient. The rise in the count is a ratchet. Once a per-cell entry is chained, the floors on trials_n and SR* hold its values, so a later return of the code to the registry-wide method cannot lower the recorded trials_n or SR*: a rollback restores the code, not the number. A fixed cut is not strictly monotone as strategies arrive (a new member can pull two clusters under t), so a night's trials_n_raw can dip a little; the floor absorbs the dip, as it does today. Every gauntlet_stats entry chained before this note stands unchanged and is not restated: 7,687 of them on the 2026-11-05 copy, recorded under the registry-wide method, plus any chained after that copy and before this note.

REFUSAL. pipeline/gauntlet_stats.py refuses to chain (exit 1, exit_reason refused_no_amendment2_note) until this note is on the chain, detected by the prefix gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-2: of its first line, first occurrence. The gauntlet worker's refusal check, the rollback gauntlet's family-kill switch and verify_registry.py invariant 12 detect the v6.1 addendum by the prefix gauntlet-protocol-v6.1: with the colon straight after v6.1; this note has a hyphen in that place, so it arms none of them. Runs without --chain are unaffected.

payload.claim: A strategy that predicts stock returns by matching current price patterns to historical patterns and subsequent returns, going long the decile of stocks with the highest predicted returns and short the decile with the lowest predicted returns while reforming the portfolio weekly, produced gross annualized hedge portfolio returns as high as 85% and gross annualized Sharpe ratios as high as 6.37 over a 1993-2025 sample of stocks.
payload.quote:
In their October 2026 paper entitled
"When Price Charts Rhyme: Historical Visual Retrieval for Stock Return Prediction"
, Hui Chen, Haoyu Liu, Ke Wu and Dexin Zhou report gross annualized hedge portfolio returns as high as 85% and gross annualized
Sharpe ratios
as high as 6.37 from strategies that predict returns by matching current price patterns to past patterns/subsequent returns. Their sample runs from 1993 through 2025. Their hedge portfolio is long (short) the tenth, or decile, of stocks with the highest (lowest) predicted returns, reformed weekly.

payload.claim: An end-to-end allocation network that maps a window of market data directly to portfolio weights via a sequence model, trained by maximizing a transaction-cost-net Sharpe ratio with concentration and turnover regularisers, can replace the classical two-stage estimate-then-optimise portfolio construction approach.
payload.quote: An end-to-end allocation network collapses the two: a sequence model reads a window of market data and emits portfolio weights directly, and the loss function is the performance statistic itself — a Sharpe ratio computed net of transaction costs, with regularisers on concentration and turnover.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Core architectural/methodological claim of the article; directly implementable and backtestable.

payload.claim: For an end-to-end portfolio allocation network trained on a panel of N assets over T periods, the effective sample size relevant to the optimized Sharpe-ratio objective is T (the number of periods), not the N×T total data points in the panel.
payload.quote: the effective sample size is the number of periods, not the number of data points.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Statistical claim about degrees of freedom in this training setup; testable via simulation of effective sample size vs parameter count.

payload.claim: In a softmax-output allocation network, an untrained model with small output weights starts near the equal-weighted (1/N) portfolio, and training proceeds by learning tilts away from this equal-weight starting point.
payload.quote:
The initialisation matters as a consequence: an untrained network with small output weights produces approximately equal weights, so training begins at 1/
N
and learns tilts away from it.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Testable by inspecting initial vs trained softmax outputs.

payload.claim: Including a turnover-based transaction cost term in the realized portfolio return objective is necessary to prevent an allocation network from reallocating its weights completely every period.
payload.quote: The cost term is what forces the network to care about the path of its own weights. Without it, nothing penalises a model that re-allocates completely every period.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Testable via ablation: train with and without turnover cost term and compare realized turnover.

payload.claim: Because a Sharpe-ratio training objective is scale-free in returns, a network trained to maximize it cannot improve its loss merely by levering up, implying leverage/volatility targeting should be applied as a separate post-training overlay rather than learned by the network.
payload.quote: First, the objective is scale-free in the returns, so the network cannot improve its loss by levering up — the leverage decision is genuinely separate, which is why volatility scaling is applied after training rather than learned.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: network weights at varying leverage levels
testability.notes: Testable by checking whether scaling the network's weights changes the Sharpe loss value.

payload.claim: The gradient of a Sharpe-ratio training loss with respect to a given period's portfolio return is reduced and can reverse sign when that period's return is a favorable (upside) outlier, meaning the objective penalizes upside variance much as it penalizes downside variance.
payload.quote:
Second, the gradient on a period is reduced, and can reverse sign, when that period’s return is an outlier in the
favourable
direction: the objective dislikes variance wherever it comes from.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Directly testable by computing gradients of the Sharpe loss on synthetic or real return series with planted favorable outliers.

payload.claim: In a volatility-targeting overlay applied to portfolio returns, using a contemporaneous or whole-sample volatility estimate instead of a one-period-lagged EWMA estimate introduces look-ahead bias that produces a large effect on reported risk-adjusted returns.
payload.quote: The volatility estimate is an exponentially weighted average lagged by one period; using a contemporaneous volatility, or one computed over the whole sample, converts a leverage rule into a look-ahead, and the effect on reported risk-adjusted return is large (Moreira & Muir, 2017; Harvey et al., 2018).

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: EWMA volatility estimates lagged vs contemporaneous
testability.notes: Directly testable by comparing backtest Sharpe ratios under lagged vs contemporaneous volatility scaling; cites Moreira & Muir 2017, Harvey et al. 2018 as supporting evidence.

payload.claim: Using three scale-normalized features per asset (window-normalized price, raw return, and volatility-scaled return) as network inputs allows assets of very different volatility to share a single allocation network without the highest-volatility asset dominating training gradients.
payload.quote: Each decision point gets a look-back window of three features per asset: a price normalised by the last price in the window, a raw return, and a return divided by a trailing volatility estimate. The normalisation is what lets assets with very different volatilities share one network — without it, the highest-volatility asset dominates every gradient.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Testable via ablation comparing gradient contributions/training stability with and without volatility normalization.

payload.claim: Training an end-to-end allocation network with a Sharpe-ratio loss and turnover penalty requires mini-batches that are contiguous in time and never shuffled, because the turnover term differences consecutive rows and the Sharpe ratio is a property of the sequence.
payload.quote: Mini-batches must be contiguous in time and must not be shuffled, for two reasons: the turnover term differences consecutive rows, and the Sharpe ratio is a property of a sequence. This single requirement rules out most default training loops.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Testable via ablation comparing shuffled vs contiguous batch training performance.

payload.claim: Evaluating an end-to-end portfolio allocation network using walk-forward retraining on an expanding window is a more rigorous backtest protocol than using a single train-test split on a fixed window, which answers an easier question.
payload.quote: Walk-forward retraining on an expanding window is the honest protocol; a single train–test split on a fixed window answers a different and easier question.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: long-horizon multi-asset return panel for walk-forward backtest
testability.notes: Methodological claim comparing two evaluation protocols; testable by running both and comparing out-of-sample Sharpe estimates.

payload.claim: In a synthetic panel with a clean cross-sectional signal, a softmax-based allocation network trained with an entropy regulariser still concentrates roughly ninety percent of the portfolio into two assets, illustrating that softmax allocation heads concentrate heavily when the cross-sectional signal is clean despite diversification regularisation.
payload.quote: The learned weights are highly concentrated — two assets hold roughly ninety per cent of the book despite the entropy term — which is what a softmax does when the cross-sectional signal is clean, and a warning about what it will do when the signal is noise.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: synthetic or real multi-asset panel with known factor structure
testability.notes: Result is from a synthetic demonstration (one common factor, 6 assets, 1400 periods) rather than real market data, but the underlying mechanism (softmax concentration under entropy regularisation) is reproducible and testable.

payload.claim: In the synthetic worked example, applying a post-training volatility-scaling overlay produced a realised holdout annualised volatility of 10.1% against a 10% target, demonstrating that the overlay mechanism achieves its volatility target regardless of whether the underlying allocation model learned a useful signal.
payload.quote: And the realised holdout volatility of 10.1 % against a 10 % target shows the overlay working: that is a property of the scaling arithmetic, not evidence that the allocation learned anything.

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: synthetic or real multi-asset return panel
testability.notes: Demonstrated on synthetic data; the volatility-overlay-achieves-target mechanism itself is testable on any panel.

payload.claim: The equal-weighted (1/N) portfolio is, per the cited literature, a difficult benchmark to outperform, and the allocation network's near-uniform initialisation coincides with this benchmark.
payload.quote: A near-uniform initialisation means the untrained model is approximately equal-weighted — a benchmark that is hard to beat (DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal, 2009).

source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: comparison of 1/N portfolio vs optimized portfolios
testability.notes: Largely a literature-endorsed claim (DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal 2009); testable via standard 1/N vs optimized portfolio comparison.

payload.claim: Twenty years of daily market data yields only about five thousand period-level observations available to train an allocation network with tens of thousands of parameters, and these observations are serially dependent, limiting the number of independent market regimes represented in training.
payload.quote: Twenty years of daily data is about five thousand observations for a model with tens of thousands of parameters, and those observations are serially dependent and contain few independent market regimes.

source.locator: Section 6, 'The effective sample size is the number of periods'
source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

testability.notes: Quantitative claim about data sufficiency relative to model size, testable by counting observations/regimes in historical data.

payload.claim: The mini-batch Sharpe-ratio training loss is biased in small samples and its value depends on batch size, so that enlarging batch size reduces gradient noise in the Sharpe loss but also reduces the number of training updates.
payload.quote: The ratio of sample mean to sample standard deviation is biased in small samples, and its value depends on batch size, so the loss is not comparable across configurations and the gradient is noisy in a way that scales with how short the batch is. Enlarging batches reduces the noise and reduces the number of updates.

source.locator: Section 6, 'A mini-batch Sharpe ratio is a biased and noisy objective'
source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: training loss logs across varying batch sizes
testability.notes: Directly testable via controlled experiments varying batch size and measuring loss bias/noise.

payload.claim: Because a Sharpe-ratio training objective can be improved by reducing return variance, an allocation network trained on it tends to favor holding a low-volatility, highly concentrated combination of assets that happened to be calm in the specific training window, rather than genuinely low-risk assets.
payload.quote: Because the objective is a ratio, shrinking the denominator raises it. The path of least resistance for the optimiser is to hold a low-volatility, highly concentrated combination that happened to be calm in the training window — which is a statement about the window, not about risk.

source.locator: Section 6, 'Variance reduction is the easiest way to improve the loss'
source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: multi-asset return panel with varying training windows
out-of-sample volatility realized vs training-window volatility
testability.notes: Testable by examining whether network-selected low-vol combinations generalize out-of-sample.

payload.claim: When walk-forward retraining is used with this allocation network approach, the variance in reported performance across different random seeds is often of the same order of magnitude as the performance differences being compared between configurations or methods.
payload.quote: Walk-forward retraining limits the damage and introduces its own problem: each retrain is a new model, so reported results are an average over models, and the variance across seeds is often of the same order as the differences being discussed.

source.locator: Section 6, 'Nothing in the model is stationary'
source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: multiple seeded training runs on same walk-forward backtest
testability.notes: Testable by running multiple seeds and comparing variance to effect sizes under study.

payload.claim: When multiple hyperparameter configurations of an allocation network are evaluated on the same short validation period, the resulting selection bias should be corrected by deflating the reported Sharpe ratio for the number of configurations tried, per the deflated Sharpe ratio method.
payload.quote: The resulting selection bias is rarely accounted for; deflating reported Sharpe ratios for the number of configurations tried is the minimum honest adjustment (Bailey & López de Prado, 2014).

source.locator: Section 6, 'Hyperparameters interact and the search overfits'
source.title: Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimisation

data_required: validation-period Sharpe ratios for each configuration
testability.notes: Endorses Bailey & López de Prado (2014) deflated Sharpe ratio adjustment as the minimum correction; testable by applying the deflation formula to search results.

payload.claim: An allocation network trained against a flat one-basis-point proportional transaction cost assumption will select a turnover profile that a more realistic, size- and asset-dependent cost model would reject.
payload.quote: A single proportional rate ignores spread variation, market impact, which assets are cheap to trade and the fact that impact grows with size. A model trained against a flat one-basis-point assumption will happily choose a turnover profile that a realistic cost model would reject.

source.locator: Section 6, 'Costs are modelled as a constant'

network turnover under flat vs realistic cost assumptions
testability.notes: Testable by retraining/evaluating the network under a flat cost vs a realistic size-dependent cost model and comparing turnover and net performance.

payload.text:
gauntlet-protocol-v6.2: Supersedes gauntlet-protocol-v6.1, chained at registry entry 68486, for the gauntlet verdicts judged once the gauntlet worker switches to it, in one thing: it adds a seventh gate, beats_hold. v6.2 is v6.1 plus gate seven. A strategy passes gate seven only when the Sharpe ratio of its out-of-sample daily returns is strictly higher than the Sharpe ratio of holding its own asset over the same days. The six v6.1 gates are computed exactly as before, keep their thresholds and their order, and keep their own fail reasons. Every verdict judged before the switch stands as it was labelled, and so does every state change those verdicts produced. Pre-declared before the first verdict labelled v6.2 exists: until this note is on the chain the worker judges with the v6.1 battery and labels its verdicts v6.1, exactly as before.

EVERYTHING CHAINED FOR v6.1 APPLIES TO v6.2 VERDICTS. The notes below are keyed on v6.1 prefixes, so the inheritance is stated here and not assumed. A verdict labelled v6.2 carries what gauntlet-protocol-v6.1 says a v6.1 verdict carries, plus the beats_hold record below, and leaves out what v6.1 says a verdict leaves out. These apply to v6.2 verdicts as written: gauntlet-protocol-v6.1 itself (the registry-wide statistics are written later, in a gauntlet_stats entry linked by verdict_entry_hash, and no gate reads them); gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-1, chained at registry entry 81246 (the floor on SR*, and the PBO null built for every family with a verdict needing statistics); gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-amendment-2, chained at registry entry 188277 (the effective trials count made per cell partition); gauntlet-protocol-v6.1-intraday-daily-marks, chained at registry entry 168621 (an intraday strategy is simulated per bar and measured on daily marks); the family-kill ban, verify_registry.py invariant 12 (from the v6.1 note's line onward no gauntlet verdict may carry pbo_family_kill true and no state change may give pbo_family_kill as its reason); and the statistics linkage, invariant 11 (a gauntlet_stats entry must point at an earlier gauntlet verdict of the same strategy labelled gauntlet-protocol-v6.1 or gauntlet-protocol-v6.2, at most one entry per verdict). The statistics job writes gauntlet_stats entries for v6.2 verdicts as it does for v6.1 verdicts, and the worker's orphan repair gives a v6.2 verdict without its state change the change it implies, as it does for v6.1, without re-evaluating it. A v6.2 verdict, like a v6.1 verdict, carries no trials_n, so the list of protocols the trials_n floor reads is unchanged.

GATE SEVEN, beats_hold: THE TWO SERIES. The cutoff is 2023-12-31, the train fence the other gates use, and every comparison with it is by date only, on the first ten characters of a bar's date. The strategy's series is its out-of-sample daily returns: its equity curve marked once per UTC day (the last mark of each date), each return dated by the later of its two marks, kept when that date is after the cutoff. A step whose earlier mark is not positive gives no return, so its date drops out of the pairing below. This is the series the sharpe_floor gate splits at the cutoff. The hold's series is built per asset from the strategy's own bars. The out-of-sample bars are the bars dated after the cutoff. The entry price is the open of the first of them, the first raw bar (on an intraday cell the first bar of the first out-of-sample day, not the open of that day's last bar). On each out-of-sample date the level is the close of that date's last bar divided by the entry price, times (1 - per_side), where per_side is commission_per_side plus slippage_ticks of the cost model of the strategy's class, read from cells.CLASSES at judgment time: one side of a round trip charged at entry. A strategy that trades more than one asset holds the mean of the per-asset levels, on the dates every asset has (equal capital at the start, no rebalancing), which is the engine's rule for combining equity. The last level is multiplied by (1 - per_side) once more: the exit side. The hold's first return is its first level minus 1, so it carries the entry cost and the move from the entry open to that day's close; each later return is the level divided by the previous level, minus 1. No cost is charged between entry and exit. When any of the strategy's assets has no bar after the cutoff, the hold is empty.

GATE SEVEN, beats_hold: THE COMPARISON. The two series are paired on dates: only dates present in both are used, and both Sharpe ratios are computed on those dates alone. Each Sharpe ratio is the sample mean divided by the sample standard deviation (n - 1 in the variance), times the square root of 365, the formula the sharpe_floor gate applies to the train window. A Sharpe ratio does not exist when there are fewer than 30 paired returns or the sample variance is not positive. The gate passes when both Sharpe ratios exist and the strategy's is strictly greater than the hold's; equal Sharpe ratios fail. When either does not exist the gate fails: absence of evidence does not pass a gate, protocol-v4's rule. An empty hold therefore fails the gate. It is a point comparison, with no margin and no statistical test, like the other gates: the out-of-sample window is years long.

PLACEMENT AND ORDER. beats_hold is evaluated after the six gates, from the same dated returns, so no six-gate value is recomputed. The v6.2 order is sharpe_floor, oos_negative, edge_decay, mc_p05, p_ruin, cost_stress, beats_hold. A verdict passes only when all seven pass. When one of the six fails, the verdict's reason is the first of the six that failed, as under v6.1, and beats_hold is still computed and recorded. beats_hold is reported as the fail reason only when all six passed and it failed. A failing verdict moves the strategy to the graveyard with its reason, and a passing one to quarantine, as under v6.1. The six-gate battery that the hand-run pipeline/gauntlet.py shares is not edited: beats_hold is applied after it, only in the v6.2 battery the gauntlet worker uses, whose order is declared as FAIL_ORDER_V62.

WHAT A v6.2 VERDICT RECORDS. metrics.protocol is gauntlet-protocol-v6.2 on every verdict the v6.2 battery judges. metrics.beats_hold is recorded, pass or fail, on every verdict whose class declares benchmark "self", with five fields: strategy_sharpe, hold_sharpe (each null when it does not exist), n_days (the count of paired dates), window ("oos") and basis, the class's existing basis string: for fx "price returns, carry excluded on both sides" (fx's hold is long the foreign currency, carry excluded), for crypto "price returns, staking/funding yield excluded on both sides", and for every other class "price returns, dividends excluded on both sides". metrics.benchmark_relative, the raw-return control of B1, is computed before gate seven and recorded exactly as under v6.1, and decides no pass or fail. As under v6.1, for a class that declares benchmark "self" the control refuses a candidate that trades more than one asset or has no bar after the cutoff: that candidate gets no verdict, stays queued, and the worker run exits 1. So the empty-hold rule and the multi-asset rule above define gate seven, but the gauntlet worker does not reach them today. The multi-asset hold is reached at graduation, under quarantine-live-protocol-v2. Raw return is not the decider anywhere in this gate.

ONLY THE STRATEGY'S OWN CELL. The gate reads the strategy's own out-of-sample returns and the bars of the asset or assets it trades: the same bars and the same date fence as its other gates, and the cost model of its class as cells.CLASSES holds it at judgment time (the other gates read the copy in the strategy's registered spec). It reads no sibling, family, cohort or registry-wide statistic. The hold of a strategy's own asset over its own window is a property of the strategy alone, so v6's founding principle, that every input to every gate is a property of the strategy alone, holds.

WHICH CLASSES. The gate applies to every class whose CLASSES entry declares benchmark "self": today crypto, fx, equity_etf, bond_etf and metal_etf. For a class with any other benchmark value the gate records nothing (no beats_hold field) and passes, because there is no own-asset hold to beat; that verdict is still labelled v6.2.

NOT RETROACTIVE, AND WHEN IT STARTS. v6.2 does not apply retroactively. No verdict is re-judged under it, and no strategy in quarantine, live or the graveyard is re-judged at the gauntlet. Every v6.1 verdict stands, including one written by a worker run that began before this note was chained. A strategy already in quarantine meets its own asset's hold only at graduation, and only under quarantine-live-protocol-v2, a separate note. The switch is dormant until this note is on the chain: the gauntlet worker reads the chain once at the start of each run, and when that read holds a note whose text starts with gauntlet-protocol-v6.2: followed by a space, that run judges every candidate with the v6.2 battery and labels its verdicts v6.2. Without such a note it judges with the v6.1 battery and its output is exactly the v6.1 output. A note chained during a run takes effect at the next run. A note that only mentions gauntlet-protocol-v6.2 arms nothing, and a second copy of this note changes nothing. The worker still refuses to write any verdict while no gauntlet-protocol-v6.1: note is on the chain.

DECLARED CONSEQUENCE. A short strategy, or one with low correlation to its asset, whose Sharpe ratio is positive but below its asset's hold Sharpe ratio fails gate seven, even though it could diversify a book. The rule asks whether the strategy is better than holding this asset, not whether it adds something to a portfolio. A portfolio-level test, such as alpha against the hold or a contribution to the whole-pool optimizer, answers a different question and is not part of this protocol.

RATCHET POSITION. This note TIGHTENS: it adds a gate, removes none, and moves no threshold, so a strategy that fails v6.1 also fails v6.2. More failures under v6.2 than under v6.1 are the gate doing its job, not a defect. The motivation was measured on the live chain on 2026-11-05, read-only: of the 894 strategies in quarantine, none of the 616 equity_etf and metal_etf strategies that carry a recorded B1 control beat its own asset's hold on raw out-of-sample return. That control is raw return at the strategy's own exposure, with the hold charged one round trip, so it motivates the rule and does not predict how many strategies gate seven will fail.

PREFIXES. Every check that arms a v6.1 rule (the worker's refusal, the hand-run gauntlet's family-kill switch, the statistics job's amendment refusals, the composer's intraday hold and verify_registry.py invariant 12) keys on a first-line prefix that starts gauntlet-protocol-v6.1 followed by a colon or a hyphen; the composer's intraday hold also needs a note starting crypto-grid-phase2-v1:. This note's first line starts gauntlet-protocol-v6.2: and arms none of them. The hand-run pipeline/gauntlet.py refuses to write unless some note starts with gauntlet-protocol-v6; this note does, but gauntlet-protocol-v6, chained at registry entry 2514, already satisfies that check, so this note changes nothing there.

quarantine-live-protocol-v2: Amends quarantine-live-protocol-v1, chained at registry entry 2515, in one thing: the graduation arm. From the first live-gate run after this note is chained, a strategy graduates only when its forward record beats zero, as v1 requires, AND beats holding its own asset over the same days. The kill arm is v1's, word for word. Everything else in v1 stands as written, and the v1 note stays in force: the cohort rule, what live means and what it does not authorise, and the reasoning v1 records. This note edits no v1 text. It changes no existing verdict and moves no strategy by itself. Pre-declared before any strategy graduates under it: when this note was written, on 2026-11-05, the chain held no live_gate verdict.

THE KILL ARM IS v1's, WORD FOR WORD. The v1 paragraphs headed THE KILL ARM and THE KILL ARM CANNOT FIRE ON ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE govern every v2 assessment exactly as written: the forward equity series, the cone rebuilt at the matched forward trade count, the burial line at its first percentile, and the minimum of closed forward trades below which no burial occurs. The kill arm runs first, as in v1, and a strategy it buries is not counted in the graduation cohort.

THE GRADUATION P-VALUE. The hold test runs only on the eligible survivors of the kill pass: the strategies whose forward record has reached the eligibility length and that the kill arm left in quarantine. A strategy not yet eligible, or buried, gets no hold test. For each survivor two one-sided p-values are computed. p_zero is 1 minus the PSR of v1's graduation arm, unchanged: against a benchmark Sharpe ratio of zero, with the record's own skew and kurtosis and the full count of forward observations. p_hold is the p-value of the paired test below, against the forward hold. The strategy's p-value is p = max(p_zero, p_hold). This is an intersection-union test: a strategy graduates only when both nulls are rejected, and the test is valid with no assumption about how the two are correlated. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure at q = 0.05 then runs over the survivors' p-values exactly as v1's cohort rule says, with p in the place of 1 minus PSR, and the strategies it rejects graduate. A book that is flat for its whole forward record has exactly constant forward returns, so its p_hold is 1.0, its p is 1.0 and it cannot graduate. v1's statement that a record with no trades cannot clear the graduation arm stays true for it.

THE FORWARD HOLD. It is built from the quarantine rows themselves, with no new data feed and no new file. Each row records the asset's price at the day's last bar (for an intraday cell, the cell named ASSET@TF, the book at the day's last bar). Per asset, the hold level on a date is that row's price divided by the price on the asset's earliest-dated row, so the level is 1.0 on the first forward row. Assets are combined by the mean of their levels, only on the dates where every asset of the strategy's rows reports; a date missing an asset is dropped, the same date rule as v1's forward equity series. No cost is charged, as no extra entry cost is charged to the forward record itself. The hold's daily returns are each level divided by the previous level, minus 1, so they start on the second forward day, as the strategy's do: the strategy's series is v1's, the daily returns of its forward equity series, and has no return for the first forward row. A step whose earlier strategy equity is not positive is dropped from the strategy's series, as in v1. The two series are paired position by position.

THE PAIRED TEST. H0: the strategy's Sharpe ratio is at most the hold's, one-sided, on the paired daily return series. Method: the studentized circular block bootstrap of the Sharpe-ratio difference of Ledoit and Wolf (2008), robust to fat tails and autocorrelation. Write s for the strategy's returns, h for the hold's, T for their common length, y_t = (s_t, h_t, s_t^2, h_t^2), and m = (m1, m2, m3, m4) for the mean of y over the record. The statistic is the per-period Sharpe-ratio difference f = m1 / sqrt(m3 - m1^2) - m2 / sqrt(m4 - m2^2): the variances carry no degrees-of-freedom correction. Its standard error se is the Ledoit-Wolf block estimate with block length B = HOLD_BLOCK_LEN. The record is cut from its start into floor(T / B) non-overlapping blocks, and the last T mod B observations are not used for se. For block j, psi_j is the sum over the block of (y_t - m), divided by sqrt(B). Then se = sqrt(mean over j of (g . psi_j)^2 / T), where g is the gradient of f with respect to m. The observed statistic is t_obs = f / se. The bootstrap draws HOLD_TEST_PATHS resamples, or P resamples in a refinement (THE FLOOR REFINEMENT, below). Each takes ceil(T / B) block starts, uniform on 0 to T - 1. Every block is the B consecutive positions from its start, taken modulo T (circular). The blocks are concatenated and cut to length T, and each pair (s_t, h_t) moves together. For each resample, f* and se* are computed by the same formulas, centred on the resample's own means, and t* = (f* - f) / se*. Then p_hold = (1 + the number of resamples with t* at or above t_obs) / (the number of resamples + 1).

THE FLOOR REFINEMENT. With HOLD_TEST_PATHS resamples the smallest p_hold is 1 / (HOLD_TEST_PATHS + 1), and Benjamini-Hochberg rejects a lone strategy among m survivors only at a p of q / m or below, so above about 100 survivors one bootstrap of HOLD_TEST_PATHS resamples could never let a single strong strategy graduate. Each assessment therefore tests in two stages. First, every survivor is tested with HOLD_TEST_PATHS resamples. Second, a survivor whose p_hold equals exactly 1 / (HOLD_TEST_PATHS + 1), no resample at or above t_obs, is tested again on the same record with the same seed and P = ceil(2 x m / q) resamples, when P is larger than HOLD_TEST_PATHS, where m is the number of survivors hold-tested in this assessment and q is the Benjamini-Hochberg rate of the assessment, 0.05. The second p_hold, computed by the same formulas over the P resamples, replaces the first. When P is not larger than HOLD_TEST_PATHS nothing is redrawn, because the floor is then already below q / (2 x m). A survivor above the floor keeps its first p_hold, and so does a survivor whose p_hold is 1.0 by the rules below. The number of resamples the p_hold in force was computed from, HOLD_TEST_PATHS or P, is recorded as p_hold_paths.

THE CONSTANTS AND THE SEED. HOLD_BLOCK_LEN = 5, HOLD_TEST_PATHS = 2000, HOLD_CHUNK_PATHS = 2000 and SR_DIFF_TOL = 1e-9 are declared in pipeline/beats_hold.py and change only by a new chained note. The random numbers come from numpy's default_rng(seed). All block starts of a test are drawn first, in one call, integers(0, T, size=(N, ceil(T / B))), where N is HOLD_TEST_PATHS or, in a refinement, P, and row k of the result gives resample k. The resamples are then evaluated HOLD_CHUNK_PATHS rows at a time, in row order, which bounds memory. Each resample's t* depends only on its own row, so the chunking does not change p_hold. The seed is int(sid, 16) % 2**31 when the strategy id sid is a hexadecimal string, else 0, the same seed v1's rebuilt cone uses. The same record and the same seed, in a cohort of the same m at the same q, give the same p_hold.

WHEN p_hold IS 1.0. p_hold is exactly 1.0, cannot reject, with no resample drawn, when any of these holds: the strategy's and the hold's return series differ in length, which happens when a step is dropped from either series because its earlier value was not positive; the price on the earliest-dated row of any asset of the strategy is not positive, so the hold cannot be rebased; the record is shorter than 2 x HOLD_BLOCK_LEN, 10 paired returns; either series is exactly constant, or has a sample variance (n - 1) that is not positive, or either variance in f (m3 - m1^2 or m4 - m2^2) is not positive; the absolute per-period Sharpe-ratio difference |f| is below SR_DIFF_TOL; se is not positive; or t_obs is not finite. Two series that cannot be told apart cannot reject. A degenerate resample counts against rejection: a resample in which either series is exactly constant, either variance in f* is not positive, se* is not positive or not a number, or t* is not finite counts as t* = +inf, at or above t_obs.

WHY SR_DIFF_TOL. A book that holds a constant fraction of its asset is pure beta: its daily returns are c times the hold's, c > 0, so its per-period Sharpe ratio equals the hold's and f is zero up to rounding. Its se is of the same order as that rounding, so t_obs is noise divided by noise, and without the tolerance its p_hold would be random. In a build fixture whose two series differed only by rounding (largest difference 3.3e-16), the p-values over 100 seeds were close to uniform, 3 of them at or below 0.05, and before the tolerance was added one such book graduated under v2 in a test. Without the tolerance, a book whose returns equal its hold's up to rounding would pass the hold test by chance about one assessment in twenty, and the gate assesses weekly. 1e-9 per period is about 2e-8 annualized, far below any economically meaningful Sharpe-ratio difference.

WHAT A v2 ASSESSMENT RECORDS. A live_gate verdict carries metrics.protocol quarantine-live-protocol-v2 and, beside v1's fields, p_zero, p_hold, p and p_hold_paths. A verdict that buries records p_zero, p_hold, p and p_hold_paths as null, because a buried strategy was never hold-tested. A graduation's state change gives quarantine-live-protocol-v2 pass as its reason. The dated assessment report adds p_hold, p_hold_paths, p, and the strategy's and the hold's annualized Sharpe ratios (the per-period Sharpe ratio, population standard deviation, times the square root of 365). Those two Sharpe ratios are recorded in the report only and decide nothing, and the PSR against zero stays a recorded column.

THE SWITCH. The switch is dormant until this note is on the chain. The live gate looks for the note once, at the start of each run: when a note's text starts with quarantine-live-protocol-v2: followed by a space, that run applies v2, dry runs included. Without such a note every output is v1's, exactly as before. A note chained during a run takes effect at the next run. A note that only mentions quarantine-live-protocol-v2 arms nothing, and a second copy of this note changes nothing. The v1 note stays in force: a run that is not a dry run still refuses to move any strategy while no quarantine-live-protocol-v1 note is on the chain, whether or not this note is chained. This note's first line does not start with quarantine-live-protocol-v1, so it cannot satisfy that check.

WHO IT COVERS. v2 is not retroactive: no verdict already chained is re-judged, and no gauntlet verdict changes. From the switch onward it applies at every assessment to every strategy in quarantine, whatever gauntlet protocol admitted it, including the strategies registered before their class had a recorded benchmark control and the legacy pooled BTCUSD and ETHUSD books, because the forward hold comes from each strategy's own quarantine rows.

THE HONEST COST: GRADUATION SLOWS. Graduation now needs both tests. Against zero, clearing PSR 0.95 on 60 days already needs an annualized Sharpe ratio near 4.14, as v1 states. The paired test against a correlated hold needs a Sharpe-ratio DIFFERENCE of a similar size; this is the design's estimate, stated before building, not a measurement. A timing strategy that closely tracks its asset may take years longer to graduate, and many never will. That is the rule doing its job: a strategy that cannot be told apart from holding its asset should not be the reason real money moves. It also removes a leniency of v1: a beta strategy in a rising market had a small p-value, and many small p-values at once make Benjamini-Hochberg more lenient for every member of the cohort. Under v2 such a strategy's p is at least its p_hold, which stays large while its record cannot be told apart from its hold's. A short or low-correlation strategy whose Sharpe ratio is positive but below its asset's hold Sharpe ratio does not graduate, even though it could diversify a book: the rule asks whether the strategy is better than holding this asset, not whether it adds something to a portfolio.

RATCHET POSITION. This note TIGHTENS the graduation arm and leaves the kill arm unchanged. p is never smaller than v1's 1 minus PSR, so no strategy that would not graduate under v1 graduates under v2. It loosens nothing. v1's standing rule is unchanged: a future protocol may tighten freely, and any loosening requires the evidence and the argument on this chain before the results it would affect exist.

payload.claim: A strategy that opens a -1 SPY short position on the trading day following a close where corr20 > X × corr60 (using 20-day and 60-day rolling average pairwise Pearson correlations across nine US sector ETFs), held for one trading day with no stacking of overlapping signals, can be backtested as a rule-based hedge.
payload.quote:
Whenever the condition is satisfied at the close of day t, the strategy opens a short SPY position beginning on the following trading day. This one-day delay prevents look-ahead bias because the correlation values for day t are only known after that day’s closing data become available. The maximum short exposure is limited to -1 SPY and overlapping signals are not stacked. The position is held for
one trading day
.

source.title: Correlation Acceleration: Detecting Market Stress Through Rising ETF Correlations

data_required: daily prices for SPY and sector ETFs XLB, XLE, XLF, XLI, XLK, XLP, XLU, XLV, XLY

payload.claim: A market-wide short-term correlation measure (corr20) can be constructed as the average of all 36 pairwise 20-day rolling Pearson correlations among nine US sector ETFs, and a medium-term baseline (corr60) as the average of all 36 pairwise 60-day rolling Pearson correlations.
payload.quote:
For every trading day, we calculate the rolling Pearson correlation for all 36 ETF pairs using both a 20-day and a 60-day lookback window.
The short-term market-wide correlation measure is:
corr20 = average of all 36 pairwise 20-day correlations
The medium-term baseline is:
corr60 = average of all 36 pairwise 60-day correlations

payload.claim: In the standalone correlation acceleration short-SPY strategy, threshold values of X close to 1.00 trigger hedges more frequently, resulting in more time spent short SPY and substantially worse cumulative performance over the full sample due to SPY's positive long-term drift.
payload.quote: When X is close to 1.00, relatively small increases in short-term correlation are enough to trigger a hedge. The strategy therefore spends considerably more time short SPY. Because the US equity market has a positive long-term drift, frequent short exposure is costly. The lower-threshold variants consequently deteriorate substantially over the full sample.

survivorship-study-v1: pre-registration of the off-chain crypto survivorship study, design doc research-layer/docs/2026-11-06-crypto-survivorship-study-design.md (Coen approved 2026-11-06). It is chained before any study outcome number exists (design s4 step 2) and fixes the decision rule below (design s5, verbatim), the frozen inputs by sha256 (design P5), the pinned registry entry index for the templates, the splice and death list, the P4 cuts, the declared halts and the declared exclusions. It arms nothing in the pipeline: only the study tool's gate (tools/survivorship.py) reads it, refusing every outcome computation until this note is on the chain.

## 5. Decision rule (pre-registered; written before any study number exists)

**Estimate.** For template t:
- `M_A(t)` = the mean of m(t,c) over the cells of A;
- `M_B(t)` = the mean over the cells of B;
- `G(t) = M_A(t) - M_B(t)`.

**The primary estimate is G = the mean of G(t) over the 80 templates**, each template weighted equally.

**Interval.** A two-way bootstrap, 10,000 resamples, numpy `default_rng(20261106)`. Each resample:
- draws the 80 templates with replacement;
- independently, draws the cells **within each stratum** with replacement: S (66), R (10), F (22), N (7), D (5), at the sizes P5 freezes. The S draw is shared by both universes.

The interval [L, U] is the percentile 95% interval.

**Verdict (exhaustive).** The rows are applied top to bottom; the first that matches is the verdict.

| verdict | condition |
|---|---|
| **MATERIAL** | G >= 0.10 and L > 0 |
| **NOT MATERIAL** | U < 0.10 (flagged **REVERSE** when also U < 0: our universe is HARDER than PIT, not easier) |
| **INCONCLUSIVE** | anything else |

Only the 1d arm decides (SV4). The 4h/12h/1h arms are computed and reported with the same formula and interval, and labelled "secondary, not decision-bearing". No secondary can rescue or overturn the 1d verdict. A precondition failure on an intraday arm stops that arm only.

**Secondaries (reported, never decision-bearing):**
- the screen pass-rate gap;
- the v6.2 gauntlet pass-rate gap over all template-cells;
- the gap in (strategy minus hold) Sharpe;
- the hold-only gap (mean OOS hold Sharpe, A minus B, no strategy at all);
- per-stratum means of m (S, R, F, N, D);
- a per-family table;
- None counts per stratum.

## Frozen inputs (design P5)

Each hash is the sha256 of the UTF-8 canonical JSON json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")), except cmc, the sha256 of the raw CMC response bytes. templates = per timeframe, template key -> sorted registered strategy ids; cells_A / cells_B = the ordered pair lists; renames / delisted / cuts / halts / excluded = the declared lists below; first_bars = pair -> first bar date of each 1d cell; data_1d = pair -> sha256 of each 1d study CSV; design_doc_sha256 = the sha256 of the design doc's LF-normalised bytes (the file s5 above is quoted from); study_code = file name -> sha256 of the LF-normalised bytes of every tools/survivorship*.py (the study code and its decision constants). Every result row carries its cell spec's strategy id, its cell's study-CSV sha256 and the sha256 of the canonical JSON of these hashes; analysis refuses a row whose stamp differs.

## P4 cuts, halts and exclusions

- LUNAUSDT: cut to first usable date 2022-05-31
- declared halt FTTUSDT: last bar 2022-11-15, next bar 2023-09-22 (a trading halt the P4 gap check passes only for exactly these two dates)

survivorship-study-v1-result: result of the pre-registered crypto survivorship study (note survivorship-study-v1: at registry entry 196930); 1d arm, the decision arm. Verdict: NOT MATERIAL. G = 0.0313, 95% interval [L, U] = [-0.0255, 0.0965], tau = 0.10 (80 templates x 110 cells, 10000 resamples, seed 20261106). Evidence only: it changes no protocol, gate, universe or quarantine record.

payload.claim: In factor portfolio construction, Boolean rules that load on higher-order interactions among signals have lower persistence and thus higher turnover than single-signal rules, and threshold (rank-based cutoff) implementations of signal interactions trade more than smooth (continuous rank product) implementations at equal risk.
payload.quote: Interactions are less persistent than their components, so rules that load on higher-order interactions trade more, and thresholds discard information, so at equal risk threshold implementations of interactions trade more than smooth ones.

source.title: The Logic of Factor Portfolios: Boolean Rules, Interactions, and Trading Costs

payload.claim: In U.S. stocks from 1973 to 2024, predicted persistence of factor signal rules correlates with realized persistence at 0.999 or higher, predicted turnover matches realized turnover with a regression slope of 1.02, and the same signal interactions exhibit greater persistence when implemented as products of ranks than as threshold (Boolean) rules.
payload.quote: In U.S. stocks from 1973 to 2024, these predictions hold closely: predicted and realized persistence have correlations of at least 0.999, predicted turnover matches realized turnover with a slope of 1.02, and the same interactions are more persistent as products of ranks than as threshold rules.

source.title: The Logic of Factor Portfolios: Boolean Rules, Interactions, and Trading Costs

payload.claim: Over 1995-2024 in U.S. stocks, 58% of single-signal factor portfolios have absolute premia exceeding their quoted-spread trading costs, compared to 24% of two-signal interaction portfolios and 6% of three-signal interaction portfolios, reflecting that trading costs rise and premia fall as interaction order increases.
payload.quote: Trading costs rise with order, and because premia fall with order, 58% of single-signal portfolios have absolute premia above their quoted-spread costs over 1995-2024, against 24% of two-signal and 6% of three-signal interaction portfolios.

source.title: The Logic of Factor Portfolios: Boolean Rules, Interactions, and Trading Costs

data_required: portfolio premia calculations by interaction order

payload.claim: Adding interaction portfolios (Boolean combinations of signals) out of sample raises the Sharpe ratio of a tangency portfolio built from single-signal portfolios, and over 1995-2024 these interaction portfolios produce returns that reject a six-factor asset pricing model, whereas conventional single-signal sorts on the same signals do not reject that model.
payload.quote: Out of sample, interaction portfolios raise the Sharpe ratio of single-signal tangency portfolios, and over 1995-2024 they reject a six-factor model that conventional sorts on the same signals do not reject.

source.title: The Logic of Factor Portfolios: Boolean Rules, Interactions, and Trading Costs

payload.claim: For Boolean portfolio rules built from threshold screens on two signals, the intersection and the union of the same two screens have opposite-signed exposures to the signal interaction term under a Walsh decomposition of returns.
payload.quote: A Walsh decomposition splits the return of any rule into exposures to individual signals and to interactions among signals; an intersection and a union of the same two screens, for example, have opposite interaction exposures.

source.title: The Logic of Factor Portfolios: Boolean Rules, Interactions, and Trading Costs

data_required: portfolio returns for intersection and union screen rules

payload.claim: An execution policy trained once on 954 Nasdaq stocks in 2019 to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread can be evaluated unchanged (zero-shot) on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs, and a second exchange using exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data.
payload.quote: In an exact order-by-order replay of public Nasdaq data, we train policies once, on 954 stocks in 2019, to choose between waiting in the queue and crossing the spread, and evaluate them unchanged on 1,964 unseen stocks in 2020-21, 2,629 stocks in 2025-26, crypto pairs and a second exchange.

source.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies

testability.notes: Describes experimental setup/training-evaluation protocol rather than a market-behavior claim per se, but is directly testable as a replication exercise.

payload.claim: A microstructure-invariant execution policy that observes a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and tick size achieves execution costs within 0.015 spreads per share of a policy trained on that same stock, with the stock's own trading history providing no further benefit, and achieves a similarly small gap versus policies trained on a second exchange and a wider gap on crypto pairs.
payload.quote: First, a policy that sees a stock only through its recent trade rate, trade size, spread and price increment (tick) costs within 0.015 spreads per share (a fifth of what learning saves) of a policy whose training data included the stock, and the stock's own history does not help it; it comes within a similar margin of policies trained on the second exchange when every episode counts equally, and within a wider one on crypto.

source.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies

data_required: crypto pair trade and order book data
measured execution cost in spreads per share

payload.claim: When measuring mean execution cost before fees, representing state in microstructure-invariant units outperforms raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors by less than one basis point, and none of these representations extrapolates to unseen spread regimes.
payload.quote: Second, in mean cost before fees, invariant units beat raw units, z-scores and asset descriptors, but by under a basis point: most of their advantage is information and a common cost scale that a learner can also take as plain inputs, and none of the representations tested extrapolates to unseen spread regimes.

source.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies

data_required: order-by-order equity and crypto trade/quote data across multiple spread regimes
execution cost measured before fees in basis points

payload.claim: A near-zero performance gap between a transferred policy and a pooled (multi-asset trained) comparator policy is weak evidence that the underlying state representation is correct, because such a comparator only detects a small share of the performance loss caused by a poor representation, as confirmed in synthetic market simulations and pendulum control tasks.
payload.quote: Third, a near-zero transfer gap to a pooled comparator is weak evidence that a representation is right: we show that such a comparator detects only a small share of what a poor representation loses, and confirm it in synthetic markets and on pendulums.

source.title: Does a Trading Policy Need to Know What It Trades? Microstructure Invariance and Zero-Shot Transfer of Execution Policies
